subjects.name: Pizza
clues: The traditional art of making its Neapolitan version is on UNESCO's heritage list.
Classic versions bake in a wood-fired oven at about 450 °C in around 90 seconds.
A version topped with tomato, mozzarella and basil is said to honour a queen of 1889.
In New York City it is often sold by the slice.
The round flatbread with tomato sauce and melted cheese, born in Naples.
subjects.fact: The Margherita's red, white and green toppings match the colours of the Italian flag.

subjects.name: Sushi
clues: It began long ago as a way of preserving fish packed in fermenting rice.
Its rice is seasoned with vinegar, sugar and salt.
Nigiri and maki rolls are two of its most popular forms.
It is usually served with pickled ginger, soy sauce and wasabi.
The Japanese dish of vinegared rice with raw fish, often rolled in seaweed.
subjects.fact: Modern hand-pressed nigiri began as fast food at street stalls in Edo, now Tokyo.

subjects.name: Paella
clues: It takes its name from the wide, shallow pan it is cooked in.
Its original version used rabbit, chicken and green beans rather than seafood.
The crispy layer of rice stuck to the bottom of the pan is called socarrat.
Saffron gives its rice a golden yellow colour.
The famous rice dish of Valencia in Spain.
subjects.fact: Traditionally it is cooked outdoors over a wood fire.

subjects.name: Taco
clues: One popular filling, al pastor, was inspired by Lebanese immigrants' spit-roasted meat.
In its homeland it is usually made with small, soft corn tortillas.
It is often topped with onion, coriander, salsa and a squeeze of lime.
Crunchy hard-shell versions became popular in the United States.
The folded tortilla filled with meat, a classic street food of Mexico.
subjects.fact: Corn tortillas have been made in Mexico for thousands of years.

subjects.name: Hamburger
clues: Its name points to a big port city in northern Germany.
Several American towns claim to have served the very first one, around 1900.
A 'slider' is a small version of it.
It is usually served with ketchup, lettuce, cheese and pickles.
The minced-beef patty in a bun, best known from McDonald's.

links.name: Germany
links.rel: is named after a city in

subjects.fact: The cheeseburger was popularised in the United States in the 1920s and 1930s.

subjects.name: Ramen
clues: It came to Japan from China and boomed in popularity in the 20th century.
Tonkotsu, shoyu and miso are popular styles of its broth.
Momofuku Ando invented an instant version of it in 1958.
In Japan, slurping it noisily is perfectly polite.
The Japanese noodle soup often topped with a soft egg and sliced pork.
subjects.fact: Yokohama has a museum dedicated to it, and Osaka has one for instant noodles.

subjects.name: Pad Thai
clues: It was promoted as a national dish by the government in the 1930s and 1940s.
It is made with flat rice noodles stir-fried in a wok.
Tamarind gives its sauce a sweet and sour taste.
It is usually served with crushed peanuts, bean sprouts and a wedge of lime.
The most famous stir-fried noodle dish of Bangkok's street stalls.
subjects.fact: Its full name means 'stir-fried in the Thai style'.

subjects.name: Fish and Chips
clues: The first shops selling it are thought to have opened in the 1860s.
It was one of the few foods never rationed in Britain during World War II.
It is traditionally made with cod or haddock in crispy batter.
It is often served with mushy peas and a splash of malt vinegar.
Britain's classic takeaway of battered fish with thick fried potatoes.
subjects.fact: It was traditionally wrapped in old newspaper to keep it warm.

subjects.name: Biryani
clues: Its name is thought to come from a Persian word meaning 'fried' or 'roasted'.
The cities of Hyderabad and Lucknow are both famous for their own styles.
Spiced meat and partly cooked rice are layered in a pot, then slow-cooked.
Long-grain basmati rice and saffron are key ingredients.
The fragrant layered rice dish loved across India, Pakistan and Bangladesh.
subjects.fact: The slow-cooking method, with the pot sealed by dough, is called 'dum'.

subjects.name: Kimchi
clues: Families traditionally make huge batches of it together each autumn.
It is made by salting and fermenting vegetables with garlic, ginger and chilli.
Napa cabbage is its most common main ingredient.
People in South Korea may say its name instead of 'cheese' when posing for photos.
The spicy fermented cabbage served with almost every Korean meal.

links.name: Seoul
links.rel: has a museum about it in

subjects.fact: The autumn tradition of making it together, kimjang, is on UNESCO's heritage list.

subjects.name: Peking Duck
clues: It has been prepared in the Chinese capital since imperial times.
Air is pumped under the skin to separate it from the fat before roasting.
The bird is glazed and roasted until its skin is crisp and shiny.
Thin slices are rolled in pancakes with spring onion and a sweet sauce.
China's famous crispy roast waterfowl, carved at the table in Beijing.
subjects.fact: Skilled chefs may carve one into more than 100 thin slices.

subjects.name: Falafel
clues: Many food historians think it began in Egypt, made with fava beans.
In much of the Levant it is made with chickpeas instead.
The spiced mixture is shaped into balls or patties and deep-fried.
It is often stuffed into pita bread with salad and tahini sauce.
The crispy fried chickpea balls loved across the Middle East.
subjects.fact: In Egypt it is known as ta'ameya.

subjects.name: Pho
clues: It is thought to have appeared in northern Vietnam in the early 20th century.
Its broth simmers for hours with beef bones, star anise and cinnamon.
It is served with flat rice noodles and thin slices of beef or chicken.
Diners add fresh herbs, lime and chilli at the table.
Vietnam's famous noodle soup, a breakfast favourite in Hanoi.
subjects.fact: Raw beef slices are often added at the end and cook in the hot broth.

subjects.name: Poutine
clues: It first appeared in rural Quebec in the 1950s.
Its name is often said to be local slang for 'a mess'.
Its cheese curds should squeak when you bite them.
Hot gravy is poured over it just before serving.
Canada's famous dish of chips topped with cheese curds and gravy.
subjects.fact: Several towns in Quebec claim to have invented it.

subjects.name: Tiramisu
clues: It is thought to have been created in northeast Italy in the 1960s or 1970s.
Its name means 'pick me up' or 'cheer me up'.
Ladyfinger biscuits are dipped in strong coffee.
It is layered with a whipped mixture of mascarpone, eggs and sugar.
The no-bake Italian dessert finished with a dusting of cocoa powder.
subjects.fact: The town of Treviso, near Venice, is its most famous claimed birthplace.

subjects.name: Baklava
clues: Its modern form was perfected in the palace kitchens of Ottoman Istanbul.
It is made from many paper-thin layers of filo pastry.
Chopped pistachios or walnuts fill the layers.
After baking it is soaked in sweet syrup or honey.
The sticky, nutty pastry diamonds famous in Turkey and Greece.
subjects.fact: Gaziantep in Turkey is famous for its pistachio version.

subjects.name: Crème Brûlée
clues: A recipe for it appears in a French cookbook from 1691.
Trinity College in Cambridge has its own claim to a version of it.
It is a rich custard baked gently in a water bath.
Its top is sprinkled with sugar and caramelised with a blowtorch or grill.
The French dessert whose name means 'burnt cream', cracked with a spoon.
subjects.fact: In the 2001 film Amélie, the heroine loves cracking its crust with a spoon.

subjects.name: Ice Cream
clues: Ancient Persians and Chinese enjoyed early frozen treats made with snow.
A hand-cranked freezer for making it was patented by Nancy Johnson in 1843.
The waffle cone was popularised at the 1904 World's Fair in St. Louis.
Neapolitan versions combine chocolate, vanilla and strawberry.
The frozen dairy dessert served in scoops in a cone or a bowl.
subjects.fact: Vanilla is the most popular flavour in many countries.

subjects.name: Cheesecake
clues: Ancient Greeks are said to have served an early version to athletes.
Its New York style is made dense and rich with cream cheese.
Its base is usually crushed biscuits or graham crackers mixed with butter.
It is often topped with strawberries or a fruit sauce.
The chilled dessert with a smooth cream-cheese filling on a crumbly base.
subjects.fact: Cream cheese, its key ingredient, was developed in New York State in the 1870s.

subjects.name: Churros
clues: They are made from a simple dough of flour, water and salt.
The dough is piped through a star-shaped nozzle, giving them ridges.
They are deep-fried, then rolled in sugar and sometimes cinnamon.
In Spain they are often eaten for breakfast, dipped in thick hot chocolate.
Long, ridged sticks of fried dough loved in Spain and Mexico.
subjects.fact: In Madrid, a thicker version is called a 'porra'.

subjects.name: Pavlova
clues: It is named after a Russian ballerina who toured the world in the 1920s.
Australia and New Zealand both claim to have invented it.
It has a crisp meringue shell with a soft, marshmallow-like centre.
It is topped with whipped cream and fresh fruit such as kiwifruit and berries.
The fruit-topped meringue cake that is a Christmas favourite down under.
subjects.fact: It is said to be as light and airy as the dancer it was named after.

subjects.name: Mochi
clues: In Japanese folklore, a rabbit on the Moon is said to pound it.
It is made by pounding steamed sticky rice into a smooth, stretchy paste.
Families traditionally make and eat it to welcome the New Year.
Daifuku is a version stuffed with sweet red bean paste.
Japan's chewy rice cake, also wrapped around balls of ice cream.
subjects.fact: Its sticky rice is pounded with large wooden mallets in a mortar.

subjects.name: Coffee
clues: Legend says an Ethiopian goatherd noticed his goats dancing after eating its berries.
By the 15th century it was being grown and drunk in Yemen.
Its beans are really the seeds of a cherry-like fruit.
Brazil is the world's largest producer of it.
The caffeine-rich brew of roasted beans, served as espresso, latte or cappuccino.
subjects.fact: Sufi monks in Yemen drank it to stay awake through night-time prayers.

subjects.name: Tea
clues: Chinese legend says Emperor Shennong discovered it when leaves blew into his boiling water.
In 1773 American colonists dumped chests of it into Boston Harbor in protest.
Its black, green, white and oolong types all come from the same plant.
In Britain it is traditionally drunk with milk, often in the afternoon.
The hot drink brewed from dried leaves in a pot, with a cup of it called a 'cuppa'.
subjects.fact: After water, it is the most widely drunk drink in the world.

subjects.name: Bubble Tea
clues: It was invented in Taiwan in the 1980s.
It is usually based on sweetened black or green tea, often with milk.
Its chewy 'pearls' are made from tapioca starch.
It comes with an extra-wide straw so the chewy balls can be sucked up.
The Taiwanese drink with tapioca balls sitting at the bottom of the cup.
subjects.fact: Taichung and Tainan are both claimed as its birthplace.

subjects.name: Lemonade
clues: In 17th-century Paris, street vendors sold it from tanks carried on their backs.
In the US, children famously sell it from stands outside their homes.
Its pink version may be coloured with berries or grenadine.
It is made from water, sugar and squeezed citrus juice.
The sweet-and-sour drink made from lemons.

links.name: Paris
links.rel: was sold on the streets of

links.name: United States
links.rel: is sold at children's stands in

subjects.fact: In Britain and Australia the word usually means a clear, fizzy lemon drink.

subjects.name: Hot Chocolate
clues: The Maya drank a frothy, bitter version flavoured with chilli.
The Aztec ruler Moctezuma is said to have drunk it from golden cups.
After sugar was added in Spain, it became fashionable across Europe.
It is often topped with marshmallows or whipped cream.
The warm, sweet drink of melted cocoa and milk, perfect on a winter's day.
subjects.fact: In 17th-century London, 'chocolate houses' were fashionable meeting places.

subjects.name: Matcha
clues: The Zen monk Eisai brought a powdered form of it from China to Japan in 1191.
Its tea bushes are shaded for weeks before harvest to boost colour and flavour.
It is a fine powder made by stone-grinding tea leaves.
It is whisked with a bamboo whisk in the traditional Japanese tea ceremony.
The bright green powdered tea, now also used in lattes and ice cream.
subjects.fact: Because the whole leaf is drunk, it has more caffeine than ordinary green tea.

subjects.name: Lassi
clues: It is a traditional drink of the Punjab region.
It is made by blending yogurt with water, sometimes with ice.
It can be salty, sweet or flavoured with spices such as cumin.
A hugely popular version is blended with ripe mango.
India's cooling yogurt drink, often served with spicy food.
subjects.fact: In Punjab it is often served in tall steel glasses or clay cups.

subjects.name: Espresso
clues: An early machine for making it was patented in Turin in 1884.
It is made by forcing hot water through finely ground beans under pressure.
The golden-brown foam on top of it is called crema.
It is the base of cappuccinos, lattes and americanos.
The small, strong Italian shot of coffee.
subjects.fact: A standard single shot is only about 30 millilitres.

subjects.name: Banana
clues: It was first domesticated in Southeast Asia and New Guinea thousands of years ago.
The plant that bears it is technically a giant herb, not a tree.
Most of those sold worldwide belong to one variety, the Cavendish.
It grows in large hanging bunches, with smaller clusters called hands.
The long, curved yellow fruit that cartoon monkeys love.
subjects.fact: It is slightly radioactive, because it is rich in potassium.

subjects.name: Mango
clues: It has been grown in South Asia for thousands of years.
It is the national fruit of India, Pakistan and the Philippines.
Its large, flat stone has juicy flesh clinging to it.
Alphonso is a famous and costly variety from western India.
The sweet tropical fruit with juicy orange flesh, often blended into lassi.
subjects.fact: It belongs to the same plant family as cashews and pistachios.

subjects.name: Pineapple
clues: It originated in South America, around present-day Paraguay and Brazil.
In 18th-century Britain it was so prized that people rented one to show off.
Hawaii became famous for growing it, thanks largely to James Dole.
It contains an enzyme, bromelain, that can make your tongue tingle.
The spiky tropical fruit with a crown of stiff leaves on top.
subjects.fact: One plant usually produces just one fruit at a time, taking up to two years.

subjects.name: Strawberry
clues: The modern garden variety arose in 18th-century France from two American species.
Unusually, its seeds are on the outside of the fruit.
Botanically it is not a true berry, though a banana is.
At Wimbledon it is traditionally eaten with cream.
The red, heart-shaped fruit dotted with tiny seeds.
subjects.fact: Each one carries around 200 seeds on its skin.

subjects.name: Avocado
clues: Its name comes from the Aztec word 'ahuacatl'.
Mexico is by far the world's largest producer.
Hass, the most popular variety, comes from a single tree in California.
It is rich in healthy fats and has one large stone in the middle.
The creamy green fruit that is mashed to make guacamole.
subjects.fact: It ripens only after it has been picked from the tree.

subjects.name: Durian
clues: Its fans call it the 'king of fruits'.
It is covered in a thick husk of sharp spikes.
Its creamy flesh is often said to taste of custard and almonds.
It is banned on Singapore's trains and in many hotels.
The spiky Southeast Asian fruit famous for its very strong smell.
subjects.fact: Its name comes from the Malay word for 'thorn'.

subjects.name: Coconut
clues: It can float across oceans and still sprout on a distant beach.
Botanically it is a drupe, not a true nut.
Its dried flesh, called copra, is pressed to make oil.
Young ones contain a clear liquid that people drink straight from the shell.
The hairy brown fruit of a tropical palm, with white flesh inside.
subjects.fact: Its name comes from a Portuguese word for a grinning face, after the three marks on its shell.

subjects.name: Chocolate
clues: Its beans were once used as money by the Aztecs.
It is made from the fermented and roasted seeds of the cacao tree.
The milk version was first made in Switzerland in 1875.
Ivory Coast grows more of its raw beans than any other country.
The sweet treat made from cocoa, sold in bars and as Easter eggs.
subjects.fact: For most of its history it was a bitter, spiced drink rather than a sweet bar.

subjects.name: Vanilla
clues: It comes from the pods of a climbing orchid.
Outside Mexico, its flowers usually have to be pollinated by hand.
A 12-year-old boy on the island of Réunion found the hand-pollination method in 1841.
Madagascar produces most of the world's supply.
The fragrant flavouring of custard and classic white ice cream.
subjects.fact: It is the second most expensive spice in the world, after saffron.

subjects.name: Saffron
clues: It is collected from the red threads of a purple crocus flower.
Each flower gives only three threads, all picked by hand.
Iran grows most of the world's supply.
By weight it is the most expensive spice in the world.
The golden spice that colours paella and biryani.
subjects.fact: It takes around 150,000 flowers to make one kilogram.

subjects.name: Wasabi
clues: The plant grows naturally beside cool mountain streams in Japan.
The part used is its thick stem, traditionally grated on sharkskin.
Its heat rushes up the nose rather than burning the tongue.
Much of what is sold abroad is actually horseradish coloured green.
The fiery green paste served with sushi.
subjects.fact: Freshly grated, it loses most of its heat within about 15 minutes.

subjects.name: Olive Oil
clues: Winners at ancient Athens' Panathenaic Games received large jars of it.
Its finest grade is called 'extra virgin'.
Spain produces more of it than any other country.
It is pressed from the fruit of a tree sacred to the goddess Athena.
The golden-green cooking fat at the heart of Mediterranean food.
subjects.fact: Some of the trees it comes from are over 1,000 years old and still bear fruit.

subjects.name: Honey
clues: Pots of it thousands of years old have reportedly been found in Egyptian tombs.
A single worker insect makes only about a twelfth of a teaspoon of it in its life.
Manuka is a prized variety from New Zealand.
It is made from flower nectar and stored in wax cells.
The sweet, sticky golden syrup made by bees.
subjects.fact: Because it is so low in water and acidic, it almost never spoils.

subjects.name: Maple Syrup
clues: It takes about 40 litres of sap to make one litre of it.
Indigenous peoples of North America made it long before Europeans arrived.
The province of Quebec produces most of the world's supply.
The sap is collected in early spring, when nights freeze and days thaw.
Canada's sweet tree-sap topping for pancakes; that tree's leaf is on the flag.
subjects.fact: Quebec keeps a strategic reserve of it, stored in barrels in warehouses.

subjects.name: Coca-Cola
clues: It was invented by pharmacist John Pemberton in Atlanta in 1886.
Its name came from two of its original ingredients, a leaf and a nut.
Its secret recipe is said to be kept in a vault in Atlanta.
Its curvy 'contour' glass bottle was introduced in 1915.
The world's best-known soft drink, sold in red cans with flowing white script.
subjects.fact: Its first year of sales averaged only about nine drinks a day.

subjects.name: McDonald's
clues: Two brothers, Richard and Maurice, opened its first restaurant in San Bernardino in 1940.
Ray Kroc turned it into a worldwide franchise from 1955.
The Big Mac was added to its menu nationwide in 1968.
Its Happy Meal comes with a toy for children.
The fast-food giant with golden arches and a clown mascot called Ronald.
subjects.fact: The 2016 film The Founder tells the story of how Ray Kroc took it over.

subjects.name: Pepsi
clues: It was created in 1893 by pharmacist Caleb Bradham in North Carolina.
It was first sold as 'Brad's Drink'.
Its name is often linked to dyspepsia, a word for indigestion.
In the 1970s it ran famous blind taste tests against its main rival.
Coca-Cola's great rival, sold in blue cans.
subjects.fact: Its parent company also owns Lay's crisps and Quaker Oats.

subjects.name: KFC
clues: Its founder first served his recipe at a roadside service station in Corbin.
Its first franchise opened in Salt Lake City, Utah, in 1952.
Its secret recipe uses 11 herbs and spices.
In Japan, many families eat it for Christmas dinner.
The chicken chain whose logo shows white-haired Colonel Sanders.
subjects.fact: Colonel Sanders was in his sixties when he began franchising the recipe.

subjects.name: Nutella
clues: It grew out of a paste created in post-war Italy when cocoa was scarce.
It is made by the Ferrero company, which launched it in 1964.
Its main ingredients are sugar, palm oil, hazelnuts and cocoa.
Fans celebrate a special day in its honour every 5 February.
The famous chocolate-hazelnut spread sold in a glass jar.
subjects.fact: Ferrero buys a large share of the world's hazelnuts, mostly from Turkey.

subjects.name: Starbucks
clues: It opened its first shop near Seattle's Pike Place Market in 1971, selling beans.
Its name comes from a character in the novel Moby-Dick.
Howard Schultz turned it into a global coffeehouse chain.
Its baristas often write customers' names on their cups.
The coffee chain whose logo is a green, two-tailed siren.

links.name: Moby-Dick
links.rel: is named after a character in

subjects.fact: Its first store sold coffee beans and equipment, not drinks to go.

subjects.name: Heinz
clues: Its founder started out in 1869 selling bottled horseradish.
The company grew up in and around Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.
Its famous slogan advertised '57 varieties'.
Its baked beans are a British breakfast favourite.
The brand of tomato ketchup in the classic glass bottle with a keystone label.
subjects.fact: The company already made more than 57 products when the slogan was created.

subjects.name: Haribo
clues: The company was founded in Bonn, Germany, in 1920.
Its name joins the first letters of its founder's names and his hometown.
Its famous bears were first sold in 1922 as 'Dancing Bears'.
Its slogan says kids and grown-ups love it so.
The German maker of fruit gummies, best known for golden gummy bears.
subjects.fact: Its founder was Hans Riegel, from Bonn: HA-RI-BO.
